paper_title: Marimba: A System One Model for Speech

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Speech applications require distinct decisions about the same short window. These include turn-end detection for voice agents, term spotting, voice activity detection, and language identification. Term spotting tests whether queried word was spoken; voice activity detection separates speech from silence and noise. Constrained answers with calibrated uncertainty can inform acceptance or deferral for review, but calibration alone does not validate an automated acceptance policy. Audio language models, including Qwen2-Audio, SALMONN, and Qwen3-Omni, accept audio and answer through text generation without separate speech-recognition step [13, 19, 14]. They typically require separate prompt and generation for each question, and their token log probabilities are not calibrated probabilities over typed decision space. Passing single 1-best transcript to text model discards the recognizers uncertainty; rare name or term lost in decoding cannot be recovered or calibrated downstream. Single-task tools do not provide shared request-time interface across terms, turns, voice activity, and language identification. Jev, typed decision model, answers with probabilities over declared options rather than free text, but does not accept audio [20]. marimba1 applies typed decisions to speech (Figure 1). frozen Qwen3-ASR encoder processes each 8second window once. Lexical questions are scored zero-shot from the decoders greedy and four beam-search hypotheses and calibrated with Platt scaling; non-lexical questions use question-conditioned head or frozen layer-18 turn-end readout. The ASR models own language scores provide language identification. We evaluate on public read speech, meetings, broadcast conversation, and noise, and on private Brazilian Portuguese medical consultations, which contain rare medication names, phonetic near-misses, and multiparty turns. Our contributions are: 1The name refers to the percussion instrument; the model is unrelated to the Mamba state-space architecture. 1 Figure 1: The marimba interface separates zero-shot lexical scoring, question-conditioned non-lexical prediction, frozen layer-18 turn-end readout, and the ASR models language scores. The shared encoder does not remove the decoding step for lexical questions. shared interface separating lexical scoring, non-lexical prediction, language identification, and frozen turn-end readout. typed task suite covering term spotting, personal-information presence, turn end, voice activity, language identification, same speaker, speaker change, and speaker count, with phonetically confusable hard negatives (including real medication-confusion pairs) and terms withheld from training. calibration and selective-prediction evaluation reporting AUROC, ECE, and accuracy-targeted coverage, with source-specific uncertainty and explicit identification of missing measurements.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Typed decisions. Jev produces typed outputs (choices, binary yes/no answers, and scores) instead of freeform strings. It does not accept audio, according to its public model documentation [20]. We do not claim to reproduce its architecture, training recipe, or RLCD. JevAdvBench examines benchmark and adversarial robustness, and TypedBench evaluates calibration, framing sensitivity, and decision cost [10, 17]; we likewise evaluate calibration directly. System One models beyond Jev. The closest speech precedent is ASOM. Frozen speech and text encoders feed shared reader without per-class parameters. The reader answers request-time choice, score, and yes/no questions in one pass without generation. Its evaluation is limited to paralinguistic emotion on MSP-Podcast, including reworded questions and new label sets [5]. Our model addresses broader set of speech decisions on conversation-disjoint splits, with Portuguese medical consultations as stress test for exact lexical checks against held-out medication terms and real phonetic-confusion pairs. Typed, calibrated speech decisions are not new. Laya provides open-weight, text-only System One models based on ModernBERT-large and mmBERTbase and uses RLCD [8]. Narrow Decision Models describes an open architecture using block attention for option-order invariance [3]. UniJev studies trimodal text, image, and video decisions and does not include audio [21]. 2 Frozen speech encoders and task heads. Whisper and Qwen3-ASR provide multilingual speech encoders whose features can be reused by lightweight task heads without autoregressive decoding; Qwen3-Omni builds on related audio encoder (AuT). marimba keeps the Qwen3-ASR 0.6B encoder and decoder frozen [16, 15, 14]. Audio language models. Qwen2-Audio, SALMONN, and Qwen3-Omni pair audio encoders with language models. They answer directly from audio without separate speech-to-text stage [13, 19, 14], typically generating text from separate prompt for each question. Option-token log probabilities can provide candidate scores, not calibrated typed probabilities by default. We evaluate typed probabilities separately from discrimination and compare turn-end detection with task-specific system. Single-task speech tools. Smart Turn v3.2 is task-specific turn-end system [11]. Keyword spotters and voice-activity detectors target word spotting and speech activity, respectively.

sections.title: 3.1 Typed questions
sections.content: The marimba interface specifies three output types: choice, yes/no, and score. Let be an audio segment, question, and Cq the answer options permitted by the question. The model receives the audio state and question together and emits typed distribution. For categorical choice question, the output is pθ(c x, q), Cq, pθ(c x, q) = 1. (cid:88) cCq For binary yes/no question, the output is probability for the affirmative answer, with its complement assigned to the negative answer. For score question, the output is bounded scalar or distribution over task-defined ordered scale. The machine-readable output contains no generated rationale. We evaluate and calibrate confidence against held-out labels; it does not guarantee correctness. The tasks are term presence, turn end, voice activity, language identification, same speaker, speaker change, and speaker count. The output format does not guarantee performance on every task that can be phrased as question. Exact medication decisions are evaluated against phonetically confusable negatives, rather than semantic similarity.

sections.title: 3.2 Audio windows
sections.content: Inputs are mono 16 kHz audio with an eight-second context, but window construction is task-specific (Figure 2). Lexical labels refer only to audio inside the selected window. The turn-end readout retains the final eight seconds, left-pads shorter inputs, and masks padding during pooling. Reuse across questions applies to the same encoded window, not to incremental streaming reuse. Appendix A.2 gives details.

sections.title: 3.3 Option representation and training
sections.content: For question with textual options, the text encoder represents each option alongside the question. The audio head scores each candidate conditioned on the same audio features. During training, option order is shuffled for each example so that class is not tied to fixed position. Training and evaluation retain option text rather than option indices. The decoder handles term questions (Section 5.2). fixed list of lexicon terms is withheld from the heads training data and evaluated separately.

sections.title: 3.4 Term labels and hard negatives
sections.content: Typed templates instantiate content questions from each training transcript. Labels follow exact token matches. Difficult negatives come from the lexicon and its confusion pairs, excluding words spoken in the clip. fixed, versioned list of terms is withheld from training to evaluate generalization. 3 Figure 2: Typed questions over one recording built from public clips: FLEURS en us and es 419 utterances (CC BY 4.0) [7] and MUSAN noise. Each question selects an interval that is read as one 8 window. Each card shows the windows label in the training-data format, not model output. The turn-end readout and the question head train on such labels; language and term questions are zero-shot, so their labels are used only for evaluation and term calibration. Binary examples include positive aligned occurrences and difficult negatives. The negative pool includes real medication-confusion pairs from drug lexicon, corrected-versus-original text pairs where available, and absent terms; unrelated speech alone would not test whether model distinguishes near-sounding medication names. We record label provenance for every example and report evaluation subsets separately by source and label type.

sections.title: 4.1 Public multi-domain data
sections.content: Lexical interpretation is zero-shot; training data apply only to the head, which uses private conversational speech and public data for domain and noise diversity. Public evaluation uses Common Voice [4], FLEURS [7], Speech Commands [22], AMI [2], VoxConverse [6], and MUSAN from OpenSLR 17 (CC BY 4.0) [18]; Smart Turn v3.2 supplies turn-end training and test data [11]. ICSI transfer uses official headset mixes and meeting annotations [1]. FLEURS and Common Voice evaluation includes only clips no longer than 8 s, so every transcript describes audio inside the window.

sections.title: 4.2 Private conversational data
sections.content: We use private conversational speech, predominantly Brazilian Portuguese, for research training and evaluation and report only aggregate results. These data are not released. We check split isolation against each experiments immutable data revisions, not datasets latest state.

We optimize the questionconditioned head while keeping the encoder frozen. Calibration uses validation data only, never the final test set.

sections.title: 5.2 Decoder scoring for lexical decisions
sections.content: Lexical questions use the frozen ASR decoder, without term-specific training. For term and keyword questions, the frozen Qwen3-ASR decoder transcribes the window once with greedy decoding and with four-beam search, keeping the four best hypotheses. Each hypothesis and the queried term are normalized (NFKD, accents removed, non-Latin letters kept, lowercase). The raw score is the fraction of the five hypotheses that contain the normalized term as an exact token sequence: r(x, t) = 1 H(x) (cid:88) (cid:2) norm(t) norm(h) (cid:3). hH(x) logistic regression fitted on held-out calibration split maps to probability. choice over terms maximizes the exact-match score, using fuzzy similarity only to break ties. Exact matching keeps near-miss inflections (e.g., coloca versus colocar ) as negatives. The transcription is shared by all lexical questions about the same window, so adding term does not add decoder pass. Personal-information questions (yes/no) pass the greedy hypothesis to an external text PII detector and return its binary answer, without calibrated probability. The release does not include detector.

Pooling and regularization are selected by five-fold grouped cross-validation on 4,000 new training clips. The selected tail readout uses = 0.01 and is refit on 5,768 clips. sections.title: 5.4 Speaker readouts
sections.content: Same-speaker, speaker-change, and speaker-count decisions use small readouts on layer-12 encoder features from the same eight-second encoder pass. Same speaker compares the two four-second halves, each with one active speaker; speaker change compares the dominant speaker in the last two seconds with the preceding six; speaker count predicts 0, 1, 2, or 3+ speakers with at least 0.5 of speech. Same speaker and speaker count use logistic regression on pooled frames; speaker change uses one-hidden-layer MLP. Labels come from human speaker timestamps in AMI and VoxConverse, split by recording. Layer, readout, and Platt or temperature calibration are selected on validation only and frozen before the test.

sections.title: 5.5 Language identification
sections.content: We sum conditional log probabilities of Qwen3-ASRs built-in language-name tokens, without an adapter or separate language head. Open-set prediction considers the 30 supported languages; closed-set prediction restricts scores to the questions options. Confidence is the softmax over the options.

sections.title: 6.1 Comparison with audio LLMs
sections.content: We compare marimba with Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct and Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct on 1,000 fixed public questions (Figure 3). Both LLMs score each option zero-shot by summed log-probability. marimbas lexical and language answers are also zero-shot; its turn-end readout is trained on Smart Turn training data, so that row is in-distribution for marimba only. marimba exceeds both LLMs on FLEURS binary term detection (AUROC 0.901 vs. 0.791 and 0.682) and on turn end (200-clip subset; 0.935 vs. 0.786 and 0.476). Qwen2-Audio is at chance on turn end (95% CI 0.400.55): it prefers the affirmative option on all 200 clips. Qwen3-Omni is better on Speech Commands (binary AUROC 0.991 vs. 0.926; choice accuracy 1.000 vs. 0.933) and on Common Voice language identification (accuracy 1.000 vs. 0.904). The remaining differences from Qwen3-Omni have 95% intervals that include zero. Language identification. On 300 FLEURS examples, openand closed-set accuracy are both 100% [95% Wilson CI 98.74%, 100%]. On 300 Common Voice examples, open-set accuracy is 84.33% [79.79%, 88.01%] and closed-set accuracy is 93.33% [89.93%, 95.64%]. ECE is below 0.001 on FLEURS and 0.048 on Common Voice. Term detection. On each private test, the held-out-term AUROC point estimate is at least as high as the seen-term estimate. This does not establish equal difficulty. Coverage varies substantially by corpus and summarizes test-set confidence curve, not policy with an independently fixed threshold. Coverage of 0.97 on curated seen terms is sensitive to test-set composition and ties. sections.title: 6.2 Calibration protocol
sections.content: We fit Platt/logistic calibration for the decoder on held-out calibration split. For the head, we fit temperature scaling on one calibration subset and compare it with isotonic regression for binary tasks on held-out calibration subset, selecting the method by ECE. Test labels determine neither calibration parameters nor bin boundaries. Coverage curves describe test-set results, not independently validated abstention policies. 9 We report expected calibration error (ECE), stratified by source, seen versus held-out terms, and decision type. We specify bin definitions and subgroup criteria before test evaluation, not from test outcomes.

sections.title: 6.3 Decision thresholds and abstention
sections.content: The consuming application chooses probability threshold according to the costs of false positives and false negatives. We do not set an automated action threshold. Deployment evaluation must specify decision cost matrix, an escalation path, and human review policy. Calibration can support this policy but does not establish deployment suitability.

sections.title: 7 Limitations and ethics
sections.content: Exact term scoring inherits ASR omissions and confusions. Private lexical results are specific to the evaluated test sets; public read speech does not establish clinical validity. Speaker decisions are per-window, not full diarization, are measured only on AMI and VoxConverse, and undercount three or more speakers; voiceactivity prompts cover five languages but not English, and CochlScene scene classification is at chance. Personal-information detection is evaluated only on synthetic, templated Portuguese speech and depends on an external text detector. The ICSI test covers only the 27 meetings we could download, and its labels mark the next speaker, not semantic completeness. Low in-domain ECE does not establish calibration after deployment shift. The private recordings were collected through commercial clinical documentation platform whose terms of use, accepted by clinicians (the data controllers under Brazils LGPD), authorize the provider to deidentify platform data and use it to train AI models. Consultation and clinician identifiers are salted before use; recordings are kept in access-controlled private storage, are not released, and only aggregate results are reported. The study was not reviewed by research ethics committee, and patients did not give studyspecific research consent. Public data retain their original licenses and usage conditions. These results do not validate autonomous clinical decisions; deployment requires appropriate privacy, legal, and human-oversight review.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: marimba answers typed questions about speech window from single pass of frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B encoder, routing lexical questions to scoring of ASR transcripts and non-lexical questions to questionconditioned head or layer-18 readout. Three results support this design. First, lexical scoring requires no term-specific training: on private conversational tests, AUROC is 0.800.92 for both seen and held-out terms, and binary ECE is at most 0.08. Second, on 1,000 fixed public questions the interface exceeds Qwen3-Omni and Qwen2-Audio on binary FLEURS term detection, while Qwen3-Omni leads on Speech Commands and Common Voice language identification. Third, frozen readout approaches dedicated turn-end model, with AUROC 0.930 versus 0.982 on Smart Turns own test set and statistical tie on ICSI. Voice activity reaches AUROC 0.9860.995 on AMI and at least 0.999 on VoxConverse, and at least 0.98 with four held-out prompt languages. Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.9660.980, above ECAPA, and count speakers more accurately than pyannote 3.1. Passing the greedy transcript to text PII model detects personal information in synthetic Portuguese speech with F1 0.904. The same evaluation marks the limits of the approach. Lexical decisions inherit ASR misses on rare terms such as medication names, and every evaluated head is at chance on CochlScene scene classification. Term detection is also the slowest path, at 2.35 p95 per question on one L4, against 1316 ms for turn end and voice activity.

sections.title: A Typed interface and evaluation details
sections.content: A.1 Output schema An implementation returns the task name, type tag, option set when applicable, probability distribution or scalar score, and model/version identifier. The type tag in the output may differ from the names used here. No natural-language explanation is required for valid result. For choice, probabilities are normalized across the currently presented semantic options. For yes/no, the positive and negative probabilities sum to one. For score, the scale and calibration target are task-defined and must be included in the schema. Invalid, unsupported, or out-of-distribution questions should produce an explicit abstention rather than fabricated answer. A.2 Window construction Audio is converted to mono and resampled to 16 kHz before any cut. Lexical intervals longer than 8 keep their first 8 s. Recordings with word timestamps yield one window at the start and one at random offset, and term counts as spoken only when the whole word lies inside the window. Recordings longer than 8 without word timestamps are skipped rather than cut, so term label always refers to audio inside the window. For the turn-end readout, retain the final eight seconds and left-pad shorter audio; padding is masked before pooling the last two valid seconds. A.3 Training and evaluation separation The train/test split is fixed before training examples are sampled. All windows from conversation share split assignment. separate term list identifies lexicon terms eligible for training. Validation serves only model selection and calibration. The turn-end readout uses separate selection and calibration pools; its public test is not used for fitting. Cross-meeting recalibration uses out-of-fold predictions and is reported separately from frozen transfer. A.4 Metrics For binary questions, AUROC and F1 summarize ranking and fixed-threshold operating point. AUROC is computed from pre-calibration scores, because step-function calibrator such as isotonic regression can create ties that change AUROC; accuracy, calibrated ECE, and coverage use calibrated probabilities. For categorical questions, accuracy and macro-F1 summarize classification; proper log loss and ECE assess probability quality. For score outputs, the selected proper scoring rule and calibration diagnostic must match the declared scale. Results are reported with source-stratified breakdowns and uncertainty estimates specified before the test run. Lexical AUROC intervals use 1,000 clip-clustered bootstrap replicates with seed 0. Lexical ECE uses 15 equal-width bins; turn-end ECE uses 10. Selective coverage is the largest fraction of test predictions attaining the target accuracy on the confidence-sorted curve; ties make it sensitive to test-set composition. A.5 Alternative lexical adaptation The lexical results use the calibrated zero-shot decoder, not LoRA adaptation, which fails the calibration and latency criteria.
